title: The catalyst calendar stops hiding what is coming, and starts naming who else moves your book
note: The catalyst card had a horizon that quietly moved. It held eight slots, and events happening this week always took them first, so on a busy earnings week the far-out entries were pushed off the card entirely and never mentioned. On 3 August eight of your own names reported inside one week, every slot filled, and Nvidia's print twenty-three days out was dropped without a word; ten days later a quiet week let the same card reach all the way to late September. Nothing was scheduled and it got crowded out looked identical from the outside. Each kind of entry now has its own reserved space rather than competing for one shared pool, so the weeks ahead stay visible however busy the current one is - and a print you own four days out can never be pushed aside by a conference next month either. The card no longer calls itself The Week Ahead, because it routinely covers six. Below that sits a new section: Read-Across, companies you do not hold whose results still move names you do. Applied Materials orders lead foundry spending by a quarter and read on ASML before ASML does; Western Digital is the other half of the flash duopoly and the direct comparison for SanDisk's margins; Coherent's transceiver volumes are the comparison for Lumentum. Every row states in plain words why it is there and which of your holdings it bears on, and any entry that cannot name one is left off. These names are not on the watchlist, are not scored, and never touch a signal or the paper book - the section is clearly marked not held, and it exists only so a print that moves your positions from outside them does not go unmentioned.

title: The paper book chart now marks the days the machine itself changed
note: The NAV curve on the Signal Tracker now carries three thin dotted marks - the dates the system behind the curve changed materially, so a kink in the line can be read against what we did to the machine rather than guessed at. 5 May: the analysis engine switched from Claude Sonnet to DeepSeek, the same cutover the Pipeline health page annotates on its cost history. 30 May: the catalyst entry path was severed from live signals after measurement showed it was losing alpha - the measurement discipline doing its job. 5 Jul: the book itself went live - everything left of that mark is a replay of the rules over recorded signals, everything right of it accrued day by day - and the quant-patterns adoption wave landed the same week. The marks are records, not verdicts: drawn in the faintest ink on the page, beneath every series, with a key under the chart naming each one. The measured curve itself is untouched.

title: Pipeline Stats becomes Pipeline health, and its cost totals get honest
note:
The page was telemetry: seven charts, twenty-one metric tiles, eight inline data tables, and nowhere a statement of whether anything was wrong. It plotted everything it could measure and left you to work out what it meant. It now asks one question - is the pipeline healthy, and is it costing what it should - and everything is ordered behind the answer. A verdict band states the conclusion in a sentence, then five cells carry the metrics that matter, each with the budget it is judged against printed underneath it.

One number changed, and it changed because it was wrong. The cumulative cost chart ran its running total across every row on file, including runs from before the 2026-05-05 pricing cutover that overstate spend roughly tenfold - so it contradicted the "Total (post-cutover)" figure sitting directly above it. A running total that spans two pricing regimes describes neither. Pre-cutover runs are now excluded from every total, average and projection on the page, and kept behind an expander that says why. Spend since cutover reads about $3.99 rather than the inflated figure the old chart implied.

The page also now says what it costs per month rather than per run. A run costing four cents is not a number anyone reasons about; roughly a dollar twenty a month is. Alongside it sits the counterfactual - what the same input would cost with no prefix cache - in grey, because it is a hypothetical and should not read as a measurement.

This is the one page with its own colour palette: five muted hues, one per metric. It is allowed here and nowhere else because the page carries no signal ratings and no price moves, so nothing can be mistaken for a BUY or for a green day. The hue tells you which metric you are looking at, never whether the reading is good - and a reading outside its budget turns terracotta, which overrides the hue entirely. The footer says all of this, because a reader arriving from the Watchlist needs to know the rules changed.

title: Terminology becomes a page you can look something up in
note:
The methodology page was six thousand words in twelve sections, every paragraph at the same weight, with no index and no search. It was built for someone reading it top to bottom, once. Nobody does that. You arrive here from a row on the Watchlist wanting to know what wide-stop R:R means, and you want it in ten seconds.

So the page now leads with finding. A sticky index of all twelve sections rides down the left, and a search box above it drops non-matching sections off the page entirely - type "peg" and you get the one section that covers it, not a highlighted word you still have to scroll to. Every entry is now three layers you can tell apart at a glance: the plain-language answer in large type, the precise rule under it as a formula plate or a table of bands, and the caveats and edge cases behind a door. Most readers can stop at the first line.

The dated method notes - what changed on 07-18, what was removed on 05-30 - used to sit inline among the definitions, so learning what an entry block is meant reading about a rendering bug fixed last week. They are all still here, unchanged, but they now live in doors labelled "Method history" with the date in the label, because they answer a different question from the one the page is for.

Two passages stopped being prose. The three-tier wait gradient - HOLD clears in days, CAUTION in weeks, AVOID in quarters - is now a timeline with widening bars in the signal colours, which is what those four sentences were describing all along. The R:R quality bands carry coloured rails, so favourable, mixed and unfavourable are distinguishable before you read them. Nothing was deleted: the page's whole claim on you is that it can be audited, so every sentence survives - it just moved to the right shelf.

title: The Watchlist becomes a page you can triage, not just read
note:
The whole book is still every name on one dense screen, but it now has structure, state and one picture. Rows are grouped under their signal with a count on each group, so the ordering explains itself and you can skip the twenty-one CAUTION names outright instead of scrolling past them. A Show row of chips filters the book, and the counts in the chips double as a read of its shape - today: 32 names, 6 changed, 1 WATCH, 10 HOLD, 21 CAUTION. The Changed chip matters most: which signals moved since yesterday used to live in a flash of colour that expired seconds after the page loaded, so you had to catch it. Now you can ask for it, and a small steel dot stays on every row that moved.

The vs-50-day column became a bar centred on the average, because it is the one column that is a rule rather than a judgment: the pipeline refuses entries on names extended more than 10% above their 50-day, and a bar makes "too far right" a shape you see instead of a number you have to compare against a threshold you remembered. The scale is fixed at plus-or-minus 20% for every row so the bars are comparable down the page, and it turns terracotta exactly where the block bites. The cluster label moved off its own column and under the ticker to pay for the width - it is context you want once you are looking at a name, not something you scan.

Two things that were hidden are now visible. The R:R column shows the tight-stop-corrected ratio with "tight-stop adj." printed beneath it when the figure was corrected; that qualifier used to hide in a hover title, which no phone can show. And when a name sits at or below its own invalidation, the column says so in words instead of wrapping a sentence across three lines.

Opening a row now unfolds a card that reads in order of consequence: who it is, the flags, whether the trade is blocked, the verdict, what changed since yesterday, what to do - then the four levels you would act on (trigger, target, invalidation, R:R) in one plate, then the evidence in two columns with the thesis pillars numbered and the condition that would break the thesis last. It used to be fifteen sections in a row, where "this trade is blocked" could sit below four paragraphs of analysis. Nothing was removed: the earnings setup and history, the risk-and-reward working, the ACCUMULATE gates, regime-change state, catalyst context and source citations all moved into three drawers you can open, so the page has a floor.

title: The Review page now answers its own question
note: The Review page used to print '14 new calls - 9 resolved - 6 went our way' and leave you to do the division. Each month now opens with the hit rate itself, with the arithmetic under it and the denominator named - it counts resolved calls, not all of them. A bar beside it shows the whole month including calls still inside their 20-session windows, so a strong percentage on a half-finished month can't read as a finished one, and the month's paper return sits in the same frame because being right and making money are different claims. The single-regime caveat now sits above every number rather than under them. How verdicts are decided has not changed.

title: The Signal Tracker now shows how much to trust each number
note: The Signal Tracker has been rebuilt around one rule: a colour means only one thing. Hit rates, alpha figures and the stop-rule lane returns are now brass, because they are measurements of how the signals did - not ratings of them; the signal colours stay on the signal pills alone. Where a hit rate rests on too few calls to lean on, the number and its bar visibly fade and the warning beside them turns terracotta, so a tidy-looking 100% off three calls can no longer read as confidently as a rate built on fifty. The five signals now sit in one row so their rates compare at a glance, each with a plain-English line saying what the signal actually tells you to do. HOLD is stated as a footnote rather than an empty sixth cell, because it makes no directional claim to score. In the paper book, the headline is now a sentence you can read straight through, and the five stop-rule lanes are laid out side by side with the real book flagged - previously the best-looking lane could be mistaken for the headline result. Nothing was removed and no figure changed.

title: Macro prints now show the trend behind each figure
note: Each of the five FRED prints in the Macro Note now carries a trend line under its value, so you can see how CPI, core PCE, unemployment, payrolls and the effective fed funds rate got where they are instead of reading one frozen figure. The line is rebuilt from the report archive and anchored to the numbers beside it, so it always ends where the printed value and change say it does - including when FRED revises a print later - and a series that has barely moved is drawn flat rather than magnified. The change arrows and lines are now brass rather than grey, deliberately not the green/red signal palette: a falling CPI is good while falling payrolls are bad. Inflation and the effective rate - the two prints the July 29 FOMC turns on - carry a rule above the cell, and each print's vintage sits in an outlined chip.

title: A rebuilt Briefing: one glance, the depth on its own tabs
note: The dashboard has a new look and a clearer shape. The morning Briefing now holds just the seven things a two-minute read needs — the day's posture, five benchmarks, what changed overnight, the one trade, the macro note, the active risks, and the week ahead — laid out in two columns instead of one long stack. The deeper study material moved onto its own tabs and nothing was dropped: a 'Clusters' tab for the per-group read, a new 'Fundamentals' tab pairing the AI Capex Pulse with the Earnings Scorecard, signal calibration now leads the Tracker, the macro trigger map sits with the Scenarios, and contrarian names sit with the Watchlist. The visual system is new throughout — a technical blueprint-style card (a clean outline with small corner marks instead of a filled box), the Barlow typeface, and a strict rule that the signal colours (BUY / CAUTION / …) appear only on signal pills, while price moves and chart bars use their own separate palette.

title: The AI Capex Pulse now explains itself
note: Every figure in the AI Capex Pulse now sits beside a plain-English line saying what it means, in one table instead of six separate boxes. The coverage gap moved below the two numbers it is calculated from, and it now says in the same row why its sales figure differs from the one above it — the gap is anchored to the last completed quarter, while the sales row is current. Jargon like PEG, percentiles and 'circularity node' has moved into the History panel. Nothing was removed and no figure changed.

title: A shorter Briefing: the detail folds away until you ask for it
note: The morning Briefing is about a fifth shorter without losing anything. The Macro Trigger Map's three always-open event cards are now one-line rows — event, date, and how many signals would move each way — that click open to the full bull/bear playbook. The AI Capex Pulse keeps its verdict, coverage-gap read, and four signal tiles on the page, but the history charts now live behind one 'History' expander. And in the Macro Note, the four 'what each scenario means' paragraphs fold under the scenario-odds bar, which already shows the probabilities. Every word is still there — it just waits until you ask.

title: New page: Retrospective — what we called, what happened
note: A new page tells each month's story in plain sentences: what we told you to buy or avoid, at what price and with what target, and how it worked out over the following 20 trading sessions — grouped into what worked, what didn't, and what's too early to judge, with the paper book's month alongside. Past months never get quietly rewritten, retired names stay on the record, and the single-regime caution banner sits above every month. Find it in the top navigation as 'Review'.

title: Readable on a phone: tables reflow, no sideways scrolling
note: On phone screens the wide tables no longer hang past the right edge with half their columns out of sight. The watchlist, the tracker's by-name ledger and its episode history, the paper-book position and trade tables, and the comparison-page diffs each reflow into stacked cards — every number sitting under its own small label — so a row reads top-to-bottom on one screen instead of swiping sideways. Desktop layouts are unchanged, and the comparison page's rationale snippets now end at a word with an ellipsis instead of cutting off mid-word.

title: Real positions: whole shares, cost basis, cash
note: Every positions table in the paper-book drawers now reads like a real brokerage account: whole-share counts for a $100,000 pot (rounded to the nearest share, spending a touch more or less), buy date @ average fill price, the current price, and cost → value in pot dollars — plus a per-book line showing the pot's current worth, cash, and open-position count (the extension lanes each carry their own compounding pot). The paper book's display pot is now $100,000 throughout, so whole shares of high-priced names stay honest.

title: Selling-on-extension trade history
note: A second drawer under the paper book shows the completed trades of the two advisory exit-on-extension lanes (the dashed curves), with exits labeled 'sold on extension' vs 'stop-out' — so the difference in selling behaviour is visible trade by trade. Advisory and one-regime, not the headline book.

title: Paper-book trade history
note: The paper book's drawer (Tracker page) can now show every completed trade: the day and price it was bought and sold, why it was sold, and what it made or lost in dollars of the display pot. Open positions gain a bought-date and P&L-so-far column. The table appears once the pipeline first exports its trade ledger; until then the band is unchanged.

title: Pre/post-market prices
note: During US extended hours the watchlist, market pulse, and today's-trade card now show live pre/post-market prices with a small PRE or POST tag, instead of sitting on the last regular close all evening. The change shown is measured against that close, matching what your broker displays. Brand-new listings without a prior close now show their live price with a dash for the change.

title: Clearer navigation
note: Every page now carries a full-width contents-style navigation bar, plus readability fixes: missing percentages show as a plain dash instead of '-%', the earnings scorecard's alpha columns are labeled again, and the day's trade idea sits under its own heading.

title: Whole-history calibration view
note: The Briefing's calibration band adds a full-history read alongside the 60-day window: older results fade gradually (90-day half-life) and thin samples are pulled toward the average, so there's no result cliff at day 60 and no lucky-streak scores. The math is spelled out in two new Terminology entries.

title: Clearer filter scope
note: The name filter now sits with the per-name drawers it actually filters. The headline scorecard always reads the full corpus — per-signal calibration is a property of the system, not of a hand-picked subset.

title: Trust meter on the tracker
note: The Signal Tracker now shows how close its own track record is to being trustworthy — how many market regimes we've seen and how many signals clear the bar — so a single-regime record can't be mistaken for proof.

title: Honest small-sample flags
note: Signal scorecards now flag when a number rests on too few results to trust, so a tidy percentage built on a handful of calls can't pose as a proven finding.

title: Simplified this tracker
note: Replaced three overlapping scoring tables with one plain scorecard plus this change log. The detailed per-name history now lives in a collapsed drawer.

title: Deterministic bucket routing
note: Which bucket a stock lands in (consider / accumulate / watch / avoid) is now decided by a fixed rule, not the AI — no more contradictions between a signal and where it was filed.

title: Trading-day guard
note: Over holidays and weekends, stale sessions are labeled 'already reported' instead of being silently shown again as if fresh.

title: Fewer false alarms
note: Retired internal checks that were wrong 40-60% of the time. Quieter, more trustworthy logs.

title: Cleaner performance math
note: Fixed how each call's return is compared against its benchmark so the comparison is apples-to-apples (matched to the same session's close).
